did_you_know.text: The title identifies the psalm as one intended for the choir director and attributes it to the descendants of Korah; it does not explicitly state who composed the words.

The psalm opens by describing acts of grace that have already taken place: the LORD favored his land and restored Jacob’s fortunes. This creates a starting point of thanksgiving for the restoration of the people and the land.
This verse uses two parallel expressions for forgiveness: bearing away iniquity and covering sins. The parallelism emphasizes the removal of guilt and the wiping away of its consequences.

After the thanksgiving, the psalm turns to direct supplication: “Restore us” and “withdraw your anger.” The shift from asking about the past to asking about the present creates a sense of an ongoing need for renewal.
The question “Will you not revive us again?” connects the LORD’s return to his people with the renewal of their life and joy: when salvation comes, the people will rejoice in God.

The psalmist presents himself as one who listens to the word of the LORD. He expects to hear a message of peace, but adds a warning that the people must not return to folly—that is, to a foolish and evil way of life.

The verse presents a connection between the fear of the LORD and the nearness of salvation, and it adds a vision in which the LORD’s glory dwells in the land. Salvation is described not merely as personal deliverance, but as a national and spiritual reality.

Steadfast love, truth, righteousness, and peace are portrayed as figures or forces meeting one another: “Steadfast love and truth meet; righteousness and peace kiss.” The image expresses a restored world in which these qualities exist together rather than at one another’s expense.

The verse uses imagery of growth and looking down from above: truth springs up from the earth, while righteousness looks down from heaven. It thus describes a connection between human actions on earth and the blessing of righteousness that comes from above.

At the conclusion of the divine vision, the goodness given by the LORD is linked to the land’s fruitfulness: when the LORD gives what is good, the land yields its harvest. The verse connects spiritual abundance with practical, agricultural blessing.
